title: Immigration Court Waits Keep Rising Even as Deportations Hit Record Pace
excerpt: TRAC data show people ordered removed in July waited an average of 901 days — up 51% in two years — even as judges completed a record 104,028 deportation cases.
body:
• People ordered deported by immigration judges in July waited an average of 901 days from their Notice to Appear to a decision — up 51% from 597 days two years earlier, according to TRAC.
  • The rising waits come despite record output: judges completed 104,028 deportation cases in July, with 78.6% ending in removal orders, up from two-thirds six months ago.
  • Wait times vary wildly by state, from 1,076 days in Indiana to 308 days in New Mexico; all but four states saw average times rise during the Trump administration.
  • The pending backlog has passed 3 million cases, with backlogged cases waiting an average of 940 days — up 71% in two years — so waits are likely to keep growing.

Records on both ends

U.S. immigration judges are deporting people faster than ever — and still falling further behind. In July 2026, judges completed 104,028 deportation cases, according to Syracuse University's Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse (TRAC), topping 100,000 for the first time in June and breaking the record again in July. Nearly four out of five people — 78.6% — were ordered removed, up from two-thirds six months ago. Immigration court officials have since revised June's total upward to 105,214 closures, TRAC notes.

And yet the people on the receiving end of those orders are waiting longer than ever. Those ordered removed in July had waited an average of 901 days from the issuance of their Notice to Appear (NTA) to a final decision — up 51% from 597 days in July 2024, toward the end of the last administration.

A lottery by geography

Where a case is heard matters enormously. In July, average removal-order waits ranged from 1,076 days in Indiana down to 308 days in New Mexico. North Carolina, Florida, Connecticut and Massachusetts also stretched past 1,000 days, while Nevada, Arizona and Hawaii were among the fastest. All but four states saw average times rise during the Trump administration.

TRAC stresses that individual judges' habits are not the main driver. What is "baked in," it says, is the time cases have already spent waiting in each court's backlog — average disposition time must be longer than the time cases have already been pending. That backlog keeps ageing: cases pending in July 2026 had waited an average of 940 days, up 71% from 571 days two years earlier. With more than 3 million cases pending, TRAC expects average disposition times to keep growing.

Speed on the front end, strain in the courtroom

An Associated Press analysis of court data shows how the administration is trying to clear the decades-long backlog: packing courtrooms and compressing schedules. Courts are assigning dozens — sometimes hundreds — of cases a day to individual judges in "mega" master hearings; more than 1,300 such hearings were held in June alone, nearly triple the previous June, according to Mobile Pathways, a nonprofit that tracks immigration court data.

At the same time, the time people get to prepare for complex proceedings has collapsed from about six months to often just over a month. The result is a historic rise in people missing court dates and being ordered deported immediately — told they have abandoned their asylum claims at unprecedented rates.

"The combination of collapsed lead times and packed hearing blocks is a schedule designed for people not to have their case heard."

— Bartlomiej Skorupa, Chief Operating Officer, Mobile Pathways

Supporters of stricter enforcement see the swift hearings as a course correction. "There's no credibility in the system that never reaches an end," said Andrew Arthur, a fellow at the Center for Immigration Studies — though he worries rapid-fire scheduling could burn out judges or risk denying due process.

Why it matters

The paradox — record deportations alongside record waits — reveals a system straining at both ends. More cases are being completed each month, but the ones being completed are increasingly the simplest to decide: removal orders, which generally take less time than cases where judges grant relief. That inflates the removal share while the hardest cases — and the millions already waiting — keep ageing in the queue.

For the people in it, the stakes are existential: a missed hearing now routinely means an immediate deportation order, and notices can arrive at the last minute despite waits measured in years. For policymakers, TRAC's numbers pose a harder question: whether a system can deport at record pace and still deliver timely justice.

What is next

TRAC expects disposition times to keep rising on average given the 3-million-plus backlog. Watch for whether the immigration courts sustain the pace of mega hearings — and whether appeals courts or Congress weigh in on the due-process questions raised by collapsed preparation times. The next monthly data release will show whether August extended July's records on both completions and waits.

nri_angle: For immigrants of all nationalities navigating the U.S. system, the data point to longer years of legal limbo even as the machinery of removal runs faster than ever.
author: Diaspora Desk
